TO:  JOSEPH HOEFGEN, CITY MANAGER

FROM:  JUDY SMITH, ASSISTANT CITY MANAGER

SUBJECT:  MONTHLY FINANCIAL REPORT – FEBRUARY 2011

The Issue

What is the status of the FY 2010-11 budget after eight months?

Analysis of Graphs

Revenues continue to slightly lag expected. General fund revenues are 1% less than expected and
total operating revenues are 4% less than expected. All major revenues are within acceptable
ranges compared to budget. The next milestone for revenue results will be reflected in the April
report, when the City will have received all annual utility franchise fee payments (water, gas and
electric), which are budgeted at just over $300,000. April will also bring another major allocation
for property tax and direct assessment receipts (fire parcel tax and sewer fee). These results will
provide a firm basis for projecting year-end revenues.

Operating expenditures are at or below expected levels with total operating expenditures 5% less
than expected, the exception being insurance due to a discounted, advance payment of a retro
deposit liability. The Police Department results reflect position vacancies and the lack, so far, of
unforeseen (emergency) expenditures. None of the other department expenditure results are cause
for concern. The April expenditure results will include three pay periods for that month and
operating department performances will likely track more closely to expected at that time.

Spot Reports
None

FROM:  ALLAN RIGG, PLANNING AND PUBLIC WORKS DIRECTOR

SUBJECT:  EXTENSIONS TO STREET SWEEPING, LANDSCAPE MAINTENANCE,
  AND WEED ABATEMENT/FIRE SAFETY CONTRACTS

DATE:  MARCH 22, 2011

The Issue

Should the City Council extend the Tree Trimming, Landscape Maintenance, and Weed
Abatement/Fire Safety Contracts?

Background and Analysis
This is the time of year when we traditionally request bids for the three subject contracts, or ask the Council for
extensions to these contracts. Traditionally we have extended contracts when we have been very satisfied with the level
of service and when the contractor offers to extend the contract at the original bid prices. In essence we rely upon the
original competitive-bid process as an assurance that we have the lowest bid prices.

The following table summarizes the contracts:
Services  Contractor  Year Bid  Amount
Street Sweeping  Dickson  2009  $85,320
Landscape Maintenance  Merchants Landscape Service  2008  $221,376
Weed Abatement/Fire Safety  Oakridge Landscape Inc.  2009  $96,294

Staff is extremely satisfied with the performance of all three contractors. Each has submitted a
letter offering to extend their contract for an additional year at the prices they provided in their
original bid. Staff would like to extend each contract for an additional year at the originally bid
prices. It is possible that we could conceivably achieve lower prices if we competitively bid the
contracts, but we run the risk of being forced to work with a contractor that would perform far
below the level of the current contractors.

In regards to the Street Sweeping Contract, Dickson has been with the City for many years and has
a specific provision within their contract to extend it for another year. We are very satisfied with
their service and receive virtually no complaints from the public.

CITY COUNCIL AGENDA
MARCH 22, 2011
  7
 In regards to the Landscape Maintenance Contract, Merchants has performed the best on this
contract in anyone’s memory. They have provided the right level of staffing to match the varying
level of maintenance needs throughout the year, especially during the springtime. They have
provided a consistent onsite supervisor who quickly learned our needs and has performed very well.

Finally, in regards to the Weed Abatement/Fire Safety Contract, Oakridge performed fabulously
and completed the contract far quicker than the allotted period during the past two years. The bid of
$96,294 was far less than the next low bid of $121,600. Staff was skeptical prior to the work that
they could complete it at this low price, but found that due to their vast experience with contracts of
this nature that they could come in with the correct level of staff and equipment and quickly finish
the work.

Alternatives Available to Council

The following alternatives are available to the City Council:

1.  Extend the Street Sweeping Contract with Dickson, Landscape Maintenance contract with
  Merchants Landscape Services, Inc., and Weed Abatement/Fire Safety contract with Oakridge
  Landscape, Inc., for one year at the previously bid prices.

2.  Extend one or more of the Street Sweeping, Landscape Maintenance, and Weed
  Abatement/Fire Safety Contracts for one year at the previously bid prices.

3.  Direct staff to seek competitive bids for all three contracts.

Recommendation from Staff

Staff recommends the City Council extend the Street Sweeping Contract with Dickson, the Landscape
Maintenance contract with Merchants Landscape Services, Inc., and Weed Abatement/Fire Safety
contract with Oakridge Landscape, Inc., for one year at the previously bid prices..

Allan Rigg
Public Works Department

TO:  JOSEPH M. HOEFGEN, CITY MANAGER

FROM:  ALLAN RIGG, PUBLIC WORKS DIRECTOR

SUBJECT:  AWARD OF A PROFESSIONAL SERVICES AGREEMENT TO PSOMAS
  FOR GROUNDWATER INVESTIGATION SERVICES IN AND AROUND
  MALAGA COVE PLAZA

DATE:  MARCH 22, 2011
_____________________________________________________________________________

The Issue

Should the City Council award a professional services agreement in the amount of $66,300 to
Psomas for groundwater investigation services in and around Malaga Cove Plaza?

Background and Analysis

Groundwater within and around the Malaga Cove Plaza has been a significant issue for many years.
Over time there has been an increase in the number and frequency of sinkholes caused by water
intrusion into underground utilities, as well as electrical failures due to water filling underground
electrical facilities. A subdrain built in the alley behind Malaga Cove Plaza in 1997 has been found
to be near the end of its useful life. Recent measurements in the monitoring wells show that the
groundwater is at all-time highs, probably due to the rains late last year.

On January 13, 2010 the Council reviewed a study funded by outside agencies and prepared by
RMS Water and Environment (RMS) on the groundwater and whether the water could be
economically used by the nearby golf course. The study concluded that the effective cost of
groundwater due to a variety of factors would be twice the cost of using potable water. Due to
concerns raised by staff, the consultant, and members of the community about the potential for
adverse impacts due to the effects of groundwater in the Malaga Cove Plaza area, the Council
directed staff to prepare a scope and budget for an additional investigation.

Staff presented the scope and budget to the City Council and said budget was included within the
City’s FY 2010/11 budget in the amount of $20,000. An additional $10,000 was placed in the FY
2011/12 budget and $30,000 in the FY 2012/13 budget, for a total of $60,000. The timing of the
expenditures was based on correspondence we received from a groundwater consultant, Ninyo and
Moore, who suggested that we would need time to monitor the groundwater for two years to
complete the study.
CITY COUNCIL AGENDA
MARCH 22, 2011
  10
 A Request for Proposal (RFP) was prepared and provided to two consultants who had previously
performed groundwater investigations in the area, as well as to a firm that distributes RFPs to
engineering firms in Southern California. We received three proposals from the two firms we were
familiar with, Worley Parsons and Ninyo and Moore, and from an additional firm Psomas. Staff
reviewed all three proposals and felt that the proposal from Psomas provided the best approach to
understanding the groundwater issues and had the best experience with similar projects. The firm
and the two lead individuals have prepared many similar groundwater models and have much more
experience than the other two firms.

Please note that when staff solicited proposals, the details of how best to accomplish the monitoring
were left to proposers as we did not feel confident in specifying the methods as we are not experts
in groundwater investigation. Each of the three firms proposed a different approach and associated
costs. Although we did not use the proposed costs as part of our selection process, the following are
the proposed costs from the three firms:

Psomas  $45,600
Worley Parsons  $16,500
Ninyo/Moore  $49,500

After reviewing the proposal, staff discussed the project in-depth with Michael Donovan of Psomas
and determined that their proposed approach could be improved with the installation and monitoring
of three wells. These wells would help calibrate and validate the numerical model that Psomas
would create of the groundwater basin. Once the numerical model is completed, Psomas can
evaluate the alternatives to remove and potentially reuse the groundwater. The added cost for
Psomas to do the monitoring is $20,700

The total proposed cost for these services is $66,300. If the work begins soon, we would expect the
services would be completed by the end of FY 2011/12. We will adjust the budget accordingly
during the next year’s budget preparation.

Alternatives Available to Council

The following alternatives are available to the City Council:

4.  Award a professional services agreement in the amount of $66,300 to Psomas for
  groundwater investigation services in and around Malaga Cove Plaza.

5.  Decline all proposals and direct staff as appropriate.

6.  Decline to act.

Recommendation from Staff

CITY COUNCIL AGENDA
MARCH 22, 2011
  11
 Staff recommends that the Council award a professional services agreement in the amount of
$66,300 to Psomas for groundwater investigation services in and around Malaga Cove Plaza.

Staff report prepared by:
Allan Rigg
Public Works Department

TO:  JOSEPH M. HOEFGEN, CITY MANAGER

FROM:  ALEXA D. DAVIS, ADMINISTRATIVE ANALYST

SUBJECT:  EMPLOYEE BENEFITS INSURANCE BROKER AND CONSULTING
  SERVICES FOR HEALTH AND ANCILLARY BENEFITS

DATE:  MARCH 22, 2011

ISSUE

Shall the City Council approve Wells Fargo Insurance Services to provide Employee Benefits
Insurance Broker and Consulting Services for the City's health and ancillary benefits?

BACKGROUND

The City of Palos Verdes Estates contracts with insurance firms to provide medical, dental, and
other group insurance programs available to full-time City employees. The City works closely with
an insurance broker to provide these insurances at the highest level of service and the best cost to
the City and its benefited employees. ISU-ERG Insurance Agency (previously Olson Duncan &
Dickins) has been the City's broker of record since 1997 after the completion of a Request for
Proposals. Prior to 1997, the City worked with ERG's Principal under the California Joint Powers
Insurance Authority's health benefit program.

In light of new Healthcare Reform laws coupled with keeping the City's health insurance costs to a
minimum, in December 2010, the City issued a Request for Proposals (RFP) for Employee Benefits
Insurance Broker and Consulting Services. Seven proposals were received on or before the close
date of January 26, 2011. Proposing firms include: Alliant, Barney & Barney, California Corporate
Benefits, ISU-ERG Insurance Agency, Keenan & Associates, Maniaci Insurance Services, and
Wells Fargo Insurance Services.

ANALYSIS

Proposals were reviewed by the City Manager, Assistant City Manager and Administrative Analyst.
Proposals were evaluated based on the qualifications of the firm and its project staff, understanding
of the project as evidenced by items offered and cost, and their overall experience. Two finalists
were selected among the seven proposing firms: ISU-ERG (the City’s current broker) and Wells
Fargo Insurance Services.

ISU-ERG, the City's current broker, proposed to maintain the City's current insurance offerings and
add pro bono components, such as COBRA administration, enhancements to the City’s Wellness
program, and access to human resources and legal compliance information. The City of Palos
CITY COUNCIL AGENDA
MARCH 22, 2011
  13
 Verdes Estates is the only public entity in which they provide a full-package of insurance services.
They provide services to one other City for ancillary benefits only. Although there are no fees
directly charged to the City, ISU-ERG earns its revenue based upon a percentage commission paid
by the insurance firms determined by the amount of premium paid by the City. The revenue is
estimated between $30,000 and $41,000.

Wells Fargo Insurances Service is a larger firm that offers comparable services provided by the
City's existing broker. As part of their service, Wells Fargo Insurance Services offers human
resources, legal compliance resources, and an employee advocacy service. In addition, Wells Fargo
has over 200 governmental entities, of those 150 are cities. As such, they have a proprietary public
sector program whereby over half of their municipal clients participate in some form. Wells Fargo
Insurance Services also earns its revenue based upon a percentage commission paid by the
insurance firms; not to exceed $30,000.

After meeting with both finalists and completing reference checks, staff recommends that the City
change brokers to Wells Fargo Insurance Services and enter into a Professional Services Agreement
with a three-year term and two options for a two-year extension.

The team of five from Wells Fargo Insurance Services that would be assigned to the City consists of
licensed professionals, educated and trained in various specialties ranging from group underwriting,
claim and billing resolution, legislative compliance, contract review, strategic planning, and
employee education and communication. In staff’s analysis, Wells Fargo Insurance Services will
provide the City with a professional team and resources to successfully sort through the new
healthcare reform laws and its applicability to the City. They have on-staff experts on the law, as
well as in-house attorneys. This will be a valuable tool as healthcare reform mandates are
implemented over the next several years.

Additionally, Wells Fargo Insurance Services has a significant part of the public agency market. As
such, they understand the many challenges public agencies are facing with increased public
scrutiny, retirement reform, labor relations, etc. Every two years, they provide a California
Municipality Employee Benefits Trends Survey as resource to their clients. Also, as part of their
unique service, they offer options to public sector organizations through their Multiple Choice and
Municipal Benefits Pool. Both programs offer a range of plan options as an additional alternative
for the City’s insurance plans. Although the City does not expect to change insurance carriers over
the next plan year, this may allow some reductions to the premiums since some of the City’s current
carriers currently are part of the Municipal Benefits Pool.

Staff contacted four city clients of Wells Fargo Insurance Services as references. All references
highly recommended the broker. References expressed a high-level of satisfaction of services
performed and responsiveness to concerns. They were described as being very attentive to both the
client and the client’s employees’ needs. Wells Fargo was explained as being an extension to the
Human Resources Department, stocked full of resources. Experience with the municipal pools was
reported as very positive.

ALTERNATIVES

CITY COUNCIL AGENDA
MARCH 22, 2011
  14
 1.  Approve Wells Fargo Insurance Services to provide Employee Benefits Insurance Broker
  and Consulting Services for the City's health and ancillary benefits.

2.  Reject the recommended Broker and maintain the current Broker.

3.  Reject all responses and issue a new RFP for services to take effect in FY 2012-13.

RECOMMENDATION

It is recommended that the City Council approve Wells Fargo Insurance Services to provide
Employee Benefits Insurance Broker and Consulting Services for the City's health and ancillary
benefits.

TO:  HONORABLE MAYOR AND CITY COUNCIL

FROM:  JOSEPH HOEFGEN, CITY MANAGER

SUBJECT:  MEMBERSHIP WITH THE SOUTHERN CALIFORNIA ASSOCIATION
  OF GOVERNMENTS (SCAG)

Issue:

Shall the City of Palos Verdes Estates join the Southern California Association of Governments
(SCAG)?

Background:

The Southern California Association of Governments (SCAG) is the nation’s largest Metropolitan
Planning Organization, representing the six counties (Imperial, Los Angeles, Orange, Riverside, San
Bernardino and Ventura) and 187 cities that make up the Southern California region. SCAG has
increasingly served as a unifying voice for Southern California, advocating for regional priorities in
Sacramento and Washington,D.C.

SCAG has been designated a joint powers authority (JPA) established under California law, meaning
that it is based on an association of local governments and agencies who voluntarily come together on
issues of common concern. SCAG is mandated by the Federal and State governments to develop
regional plans for transportation, growth management, housing development, air quality and other
issues of regional significance.

In Southern California, SCAG is the forum where local leaders converge to discuss common problems
and develop common solutions to shared regional challenges. In order to ensure that Palos Verdes
Estates has a voice in important issues that SCAG is currently mandated to oversee, it is recommended
that the City become a member.

Discussion:

To date, the City of Palos Verdes Estates has not chosen to become a member of SCAG.
Organizations such as SCAG allow smaller municipalities to have a larger voice when it comes to
regional issues; as well as State and Federal issues.

The core functions of SCAG include:

a. Exchange of objective planning information that affect local governments;
CITY COUNCIL AGENDA
MARCH 22, 2011
  16
 b. Identification and study of problems and the making of appropriate policy or action
recommendations;
c. Review and/or develop governmental proposals and proposals creating agencies of regional scope,
and the making of appropriate policy or action recommendations concerning the need for such units or
agencies;
d. Consider questions of common interest and concern to members of the Association and may develop
policy and action recommendations of an advisory nature only; and;
e. Act upon any matter to the extent and manner required, permitted or authorized by the joint powers
agreements, State or Federal law, or the regulations adopted pursuant to any such law.

Under Federal and State law, SCAG is designated as a Metropolitan Planning Organization (MPO), a
Regional Transportation Planning Agency (RTPA) and a Council of Governments (COG). As a
designated MPO under Federal law, SCAG is responsible for developing and adopting a long-range
Regional Transportation Plan (RTP) every four (4) years; and developing and approving a short-term
Regional Transportation Improvement Program (RTIP) every two (2) years. The RTP serves as a basis
for transportation decision making in the region. If a particular highway, road or transit improvement
is not represented in the RTP, it cannot receive State or Federal funds. The RTIP is a plan which
determines and prioritizes how much Federal funding State and local agencies receive in a five-year
time span.

Under State law as a Council of Governments (COG), SCAG is responsible for developing a portion of
the Air Quality Management Plan (AQMP) prepared by the South Coast Air Quality Management
District (SCAQMD); a Regional Housing Needs Assessment (RHNA) to determine each jurisdiction’s
fair share of the region’s future housing needs, as determined by the State Department of Housing and
Community Development; pursuant the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) undertakes the
appropriate environmental review for the RTP and RTIP; and may prepare a regional hazardous waste
management plan to identify hazardous waste management issues at the regional levels.

When a jurisdiction joins SCAG, a new seat is created on the SCAG General Assembly.
Representatives to the Assembly elect officers, adopt SCAG’s annual work program, set the agency’s
planning and policy priorities, and approve the study of specific problems, programs and other matters
that concern the region. The City would designate one delegate and one alternate from the City
Council to sit on the General Assembly. SCAG facilitates and encourages coordination and
cooperation among multiple levels of government for the greater benefit of all. By joining SCAG, the
City would be guaranteed a seat at the table where solutions to regional problems are formulated and
later implemented.

Fiscal Impact:

Based on the City of Palos Verdes Estates population, the FY 2010-11 membership dues are $1,288.
Since the City would be joining mid-year, the membership dues are prorated in the amount of $322.08
for April 1, 2011 – June 30, 2011.

Recommendation:
CITY COUNCIL AGENDA
MARCH 22, 2011
  17
 That the City Council authorize (1) the City Manager to submit the City’s request for membership and
pay membership dues to the Southern California Association of Governments (SCAG); (2) the City
Manager to sign the SCAG Joint Powers Agreement that is necessary for membership; and (3) the
Mayor to appoint a delegate and alternate representative to the SCAG General Assembly from the City
Council.

AWARD OF PROFESSIONAL SERVICES AGREEMENT TO PSOMAS FOR
GROUNDWATER INVESTIGATION SERVICES IN AND AROUND MALAGA COVE
PLAZA

Public Works Director Rigg reported that groundwater within and around Malaga Cove Plaza has been
a significant issue for many years. Over time there has been an increase in the number and frequency
of sinkholes caused by water intrusion into underground utilities as well as multiple electrical failures
due to water filling underground electrical facilities. A subdrain built in the alley behind the Malaga
Cove Plaza in 1997 has been found to be near the end of its useful life. There have been failures in the
subdrain due to dirt entering the subdrain which requires periodic clearing. Groundwater is at an all-
time high most likely due to the heavy rains late in 2010. The peak water level usually happens in June
or July 4-5 months after the heavy rainfall. In January 2010 the Council reviewed a study funded by
outside agencies regarding whether groundwater could be used by the nearby golf course. It was found
to be cost prohibitive at twice the cost of potable water. Council directed staff to prepare a scope and
budget for an additional investigation. A Request for Proposal (RFP) was issued. A total of three
proposals were received and reviewed. Psomas was found to be the best qualified firm with the best
people and most representative projects of the type of work required. The original price proposed was
for $45,600 and staff asked Psomas to add groundwater monitoring to validate and calibrate their
numerical model of the groundwater. The added cost for the monitoring is $20,700 for a total of
$66,300.

 Mayor Rea asked why one of the bids, for $16,500, was so low. Director Rigg said the City did not
know what the scope of the project would be and left it up to the bidders. The low bid proposal was
significantly inadequate compared to the two other proposals.

Mayor Rea asked if there is enough money in the budget to cover the project. Director Rigg said a
budget adjustment of $6,300 would be required.

Ray Burns has lived in PVE on and off for 57 years and is the managing general partner with Peninsula
Investment Company that built the Post Office building and the building next to it in the early 1960’s.
The aquifer flows down towards the commercial buildings and the adjacent residential area. In (1997)
the subdrain was installed behind the commercial properties in the Plaza. This drain system is no
longer able to function at the level of its original design. In his opinion it is essential that the City have
a thorough understanding of the groundwater issues and the means of mitigating the adverse affects to
the City. He encouraged the Council to approve the agreement with Psomas.

Mike Donavan, the senior hydro-geologist with Psomas, said while responding to the proposal he
looked at some of the available information and some good work was conducted years ago by a
graduate student working with the then Public Works Engineer for the City. He said he and Psomas
are very capable of doing the project which is very interesting and he believes they can solve the
problem for PVE in Malaga Cove Plaza.

Councilmember Goodhart asked how the City can keep the costs in check for this project. Director
Rigg said there is no way to plan for that at this time. The hope is that the aquifer operates such that
the water from the Golf Club property flows down to Malaga Cove Plaza and the City could work with
the Golf Club to develop a well system on the Golf Club site to use for irrigation. If the aquifer has
developed in a way that the two areas are not connected who knows what the cost could be. Once a it
is determined how to fix the water levels, staff will forward recommendations to the Council.

Councilmember Humphrey was in favor of the recommendation. The City has been dealing with this
issue for years.

Mayor Pro Tem Bird was also in favor of the recommendation. He was impressed with the level of
relevant project experience of Psomas and Mr. Donavan.

Mayor Rea was also in favor of the recommendation. He was unhappy to learn from the previous
water study that it was not economically feasible to pump the water up the hill to the Golf Club. So
putting a well on the golf course might be a better solution if that is a feasible solution.

It was moved by Councilmember Humphrey, seconded by Councilmember Goodhart and unanimously
approved to award a professional services agreement in the amount of $66,300 to Psomas for
groundwater investigation services in and around Malaga Cove Plaza. (4-0, Perkins absent)

AWARD OF PROFESSIONAL SERVICES AGREEMENT FOR EMPLOYEE BENEFITS
INSURANCE BROKER AND CONSULTING SERVICES FOR THE CITY’S HEALTH AND
ANCILLARY BENEFITS

CITY COUNCIL  3
March 22, 2011
 Administrative Analyst Alexa Davis reported that the City uses an insurance broker to identify and
negotiate core and ancillary benefits available to full-time employees. The City has worked with ISU
ERG as the insurance broker for the past 13 years. As the City has not solicited proposals in 13 years
and due to new health care regulations, the City issued an RFP for employee benefits and insurance
broker services and consulting services. Seven firms responded by the due date of January 26, 2011.
The proposals were reviewed and evaluated by staff based upon the qualifications of the firm, staff that
would be assigned to PVE, the understanding of the project as evidenced by the services and
insurances offered and associated costs and the firms overall experience. The two finalists selected
were ISU ERG and Wells Fargo Insurance Services. Staff met with both firms and completed
reference checks. ISU ERG proposed to maintain the City’s current insurance offering and added
various pro bono components such as COBRA administration, enhancements to the employee
Wellness Program and access to human resources and legal compliance information. ISU ERG does
not provide service to many public entities. They do not charge PVE directly for their services, but
rather earn their revenue based upon a commission paid directly from the insurance carriers. This
revenue is estimated to be $31,000 to $41,000 per year. The other finalist was Wells Fargo Insurance
Services which is a national firm that proposed comparable services to what is currently provided to the
City. Wells Fargo additionally proposed human resource and legal compliance information as well as
an employee advocacy service. Wells Fargo also earns revenue based upon a percentage paid by the
insurance carriers and they propose not to exceed $30,000. Wells Fargo provides insurance services to
up to 150 cities in California. With a strong focus on public agencies, they are able to offer a
proprietary public sector program with a range of plans and carriers. The City does not anticipate
changing insurance carriers over the next plan year which may allow a reduction in part of the
premium as some of the City’s current plans already exist in their municipal pools. The Wells Fargo
team assigned to the PVE account includes high-level professionals that are licensed in various
specialties and more specifically they are able to provide thorough resources needed to successfully
navigate the new health care reform law and its applicability to PVE. They were highly rated by their
references for their service and responsiveness.

Andrew Scillan, Managing Director of Wells Fargo Insurance Services, thanked the Council for the
opportunity to handle the City’s insurance programs and to be a trusted advisor. Regarding the team
assigned to PVE, he has known the lead consultant, Gary Delaney, for 20 years. They work for
numerous cities in the area with numerous attorneys on staff to help PVE through the health care
reform laws as they change and evolve. It is a robust team with lead consultants who will help with
bargaining unit issues, claim issues, advocacy, etc.

Councilmember Goodhart felt it was a great idea in the ever-changing insurance environment to have a
firm whose business it is to keep up with such things.

Councilmember Humphrey said the previous brokers served PVE well for many years. The staff
conducted a thorough analysis and she hopes this will be a supportive, productive relationship for the
staff and employees.

It was moved by Mayor Pro Tem Bird, seconded by Councilmember Humphrey and unanimously
approved to award a professional services agreement to Wells Fargo Insurance Services to provide
employee benefits insurance broker and consulting services for the City’s health and ancillary benefits.
(4-0, Perkins absent)

 APPROVAL OF THE JOINT POWERS AGREEMENT FOR MEMBERSHIP IN THE
SOUTHERN CALIFORNIA ASSOCIATION OF GOVERNMENTS (SCAG)

City Manager Hoefgen reported SCAG is a joint powers authority with boundaries covering 190 cities
in six counties. It is a regional government that intends to focus on those issues that are common
among different jurisdictions. The staff report outlined the different responsibilities and projects that
they are mandated to perform including transportation planning, growth management and forecasting
as well as focusing on housing development throughout their regional planning area. Over the past few
months, SCAG has made a concerted effort to get the few remaining cities that are not members of
SCAG to join. One by one these cities are opting to join SCAG. Staff has had many discussions with
SCAG staff describing why PVE has not been a member conveying that PVE is a built-out community
that was master planned many years ago. Many of the things that fall in SCAG’s jurisdiction have not
been of significant importance to PVE. There is a new development that has prompted PVE to look at
being a member of SCAG. SCAG is now citing authority that they believe they have in State law to
collect payments from non-member cities for work that SCAG is mandated to complete related to
preparation of the Regional Housing Needs Assessment (RHNA) analysis. The RHNA is a state
mandated annual analysis that SCAG completes for each city within their jurisdiction including PVE.
Staff has verified with the City Attorney that SCAG does have the authority to extract fees from the
non-member cities for preparation of the RHNA. The fees that are charged need to reflect the
reasonable actual cost of preparing the RHNA. Staff looked into this with SCAG and understands that
last year SCAG incurred $2.2 million in costs related to the preparation of the RHNA throughout their
six county planning area. SCAG has divided the $2.2 million cost amongst each of their cities which is
about $12,000 per agency. The options to PVE are: 1) retain status and remain a non-member of
SCAG and potentially be liable for the payment of the $12,000 fair share fee for the preparation of the
RHNA, 2) become a member of SCAG at a fee of $1,300 per year. PVE contacted other cities who
are not members of SCAG and all are opting to join SCAG rather than pay the RHNA fee. City
Manager Hoefgen reviewed the issue in February with then Mayor Humphrey and Mayor Pro Tem Rea
and they concluded that joining SCAG at a cost of $1,300 would be preferable to paying $12,000 per
year. This year’s membership fee would be prorated at $322 for April to June 2011.

Mayor Rea said SCAG has chosen to waive the RHNA fee for members which would leave only two
cities in Los Angeles County, with PVE being one, which would have to pay a RHNA fee if PVE
chose not to join. He did not see any great benefit to PVE being a member of SCAG, but with the
economic pressure from SCAG it would be better to join.

Councilmember Humphrey agreed with Mayor Rea. She sees tremendous benefits from the fees PVE
pays for membership in the League of California Cities and the South Bay Association of Governments
but she is not sure what benefit a SCAG membership would provide. She asked how PVE could get
out of its membership in the future if the city was no longer interested in being a member. City
Manager Hoefgen said that PVE would notify SCAG and not pay the dues. Councilmember
Humphrey would like staff to keep an eye on the issues and positions being taken by SCAG to be sure
they are in the best interests of PVE.

Mayor Pro Tem Bird asked the City Attorney if it is lawful for SCAG to assess PVE $12,000 annually
for a report that is prepared every five years even though PVE is an independent city. Attorney Hogin
said state law does authorize SCAG to charge reasonable costs for the preparation of the RHNA

 analysis. Mayor Pro Tem Bird questioned the premise that the value of the information is $12,000 per
year, but if you join the organization at a fee of $1,300 the information is free. City Manager Hoefgen
said the dues are calculated using population and some cities are paying far more than $12,000 for their
SCAG membership. Mayor Pro Tem Bird was amazed that at some time SCAG was successful in
lobbying the state legislature to make SCAG the point guard for preparation of the RHNA for which
they can force cities to pay for through forced membership in SCAG. He said that is effective
lobbying.

Councilmember Goodhart agreed that in the past PVE did not see the value of a membership in SCAG,
but a couple of things have changed. The passage of AB32 and SB375, the environmental quality
legislation has given SCAG more involvement and authority in transportation and air quality planning.
It is all very complex and interrelated. He views the membership as protection for PVE. If PVE is not
part of the process and monitoring the information being used for the various calculations, it would be
hard to change things down the road and PVE would have to live with it. He supports approving
membership in SCAG.

Councilmember Humphrey was not sure that SCAG would accept any corrected information in her
experience.

Mayor Rea asked about language in the by-laws – it said the City shall have one official representative
and one alternate in the General Assembly. City Manager Hoefgen said he asked the Executive
Director of SCAG if participation is mandatory and was told there is no requirement to designate a
representative. A member can only attend and participate in the General Assembly if the representative
has been designated by the City Council.

Mayor Rea asked if there is anyone in the surrounding cities that is a member of PVE’s designated
regional council. City Manager Hoefgen said Judy Mitchell of RHE is on the regional council.

It was moved by Mayor Pro Tem Bird, seconded by Councilmember Goodhart and unanimously
approved to authorize the Mayor to sign the SCAG Joint Powers Agreement. (4-0, Perkins absent)

MAYOR & CITY COUNCILMEMBERS’ REPORTS

Mayor Rea announced the City Council Committee and Liaison Assignments for 2011-12. He said he,
in consultation with Attorney Hogin, completely revamped the listings. He divided the assignments
into three categories: 1) Standing Committees, 2) Ad-Hoc Committees, and 3) Liaison Assignments.
He said he removed the liaisons to the School District, Library District and PV Homes Association. He
also removed the rotating assignments of Council members to attend the Planning Commission, Traffic
Safety Committee and Parklands Committee meetings as there are official minutes taken at those
meetings that can be referred to when needed. He removed the Disaster District Program liaisons from
the list as the program has recently launched and can now be handled by staff. He explained the reason
for him being assigned as the only liaison to the PV Beach & Athletic Club. As Council members
Perkins and Goodhart recused themselves from discussions regarding the PVBAC, there are only three
Council members left to vote on any PVBAC matters. He felt it better to have only one liaison attend
any meetings and report back to the remaining two Council members.

Councilmember Humphrey thought the changes to the Liaison Assignments were good and she
commended Mayor Rea on making the changes.

Councilmember Bird said the City is fortunate to have such terrific commissioners and committee
members serving on these committees and this shows the Council’s confidence in them.

It was moved by Councilmember Humphrey, seconded by Councilmember Goodhart and unanimously
approved to receive and file the report. (4-0, Perkins absent)
